c.tagline: A slender coral atoll on the frontline of climate change.

taxi.fareNote: Shared taxis and minibuses charge flat per-stage fares along the single main road; agree the fare before boarding since meters aren't used.

emergency.note: Health facilities are very basic (the modest Tungaru Central Hospital in Bairiki); serious illness or injury usually requires evacuation to Fiji or Australia, so travel insurance with medevac coverage is essential.

hood_landmark.Bikenibeu: University of the South Pacific Kiribati Campus, Bikenibeu
hood_landmark.North Tarawa: Tabon Te Keekee Eco-Lodge, Abatao Island

hood_desc: The gritty port islet at the atoll's western tip, packed with WWII bunkers and gun emplacements around Red Beach; suits history buffs and budget travelers who don't mind a livelier, more urban feel.
A quieter, mid-strip residential district anchored by the University of the South Pacific campus; suits longer-stay visitors, students, and those wanting distance from the busiest parts of town.
Home to Kiribati's Parliament and a mix of government compounds and family homes; a convenient, central base for business travelers, consultants, and NGO staff.
The easternmost developed stretch, wrapped around the international airport; practical for transit passengers or anyone needing an easy early-morning departure.
A string of quieter, boat-accessible islets north of the main causeway, with eco-lodges and traditional village life; ideal for travelers wanting a slower, nature-focused stay.

water.note: Tap water is not recommended for drinking; use bottled or treated water.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash (AUD) directly to the driver or conductor; there is no ticketing system or fare card. Short hops cost roughly AUD 1-2 regardless of distance along the route, with longer trips (e.g. Bairiki to Bonriki) costing a little more.
transit.hours: Minibuses and shared taxis generally run from around 6am to 9-10pm; there is no late-night or 24-hour service.
transit.note: There is no railway, ferry, or formal transit authority within South Tarawa; the single ~32km road connecting Betio to Tanaea is the main corridor, served entirely by privately operated minibuses and shared taxis.

bus: Privately operated shared minibuses running the length of the main South Tarawa road between Betio and Tanaea
ferry: Government-operated inter-island ferries (e.g. MV Moamoa) connecting Betio to the outer Gilbert Islands

airport.name: Bonriki International Airport (TRW)
rentals: No international rental chains operate; vehicles can be hired informally through hotels (e.g. Otintaai Hotel) or local operators

tip.r: Tipping is not part of local custom in Kiribati; it's neither expected nor commonly practiced, though rounding up for good service at hotels is fine.

food.name: Palusami
food.desc: Young taro or pumpkin leaves parcelled up with thick coconut cream and baked slowly until they collapse into a rich, silky green pudding.

places.name: Babes Place
places.note: Cultural institution known for locally sourced ingredients and proper traditional Kiribati cooking.

places.name: Otintaai Hotel Restaurant
places.note: The main hotel dining room, mixing island staples with international dishes; palusami on traditional nights.

places.name: Bairiki Market food stalls
places.note: South Tarawa's main market, with prepared-food stalls selling coconut-cream dishes at local prices.

food.name: Coconut Crab (Te Ai)
food.desc: The giant land crab that cracks coconuts with its claws, split and grilled or cooked in its own fat and coconut cream. Rare, seasonal and prized.

places.name: Ocean Family Seafood
places.note: Seafood-focused kitchen and bar; pricey by Kiribati standards but the reliable seafood address.

places.name: Babes Place
places.note: Sources local catch directly; coconut crab appears when islanders bring it in from the outer islets.

places.name: Betio Market
places.note: Port-side market where crab and lagoon catch are traded; ask early in the day.

food.name: Grilled Tuna and Raw Fish
food.desc: Skipjack and yellowfin grilled over coconut husks, or cubed raw with lime, coconut cream and onion. The everyday protein of an atoll nation.

places.name: Ocean Family Seafood
places.note: Best-known seafood restaurant on the atoll, with fish landed the same morning.

places.name: Chatterbox Cafe
places.note: Highly rated cafe doing fresh fish plates and good coffee; popular with residents and visitors.

places.name: Betio Market
places.note: Fish stalls beside the harbour sell tuna straight off the boats, often grilled to order nearby.

food.name: Te Buatoro (Fermented Breadfruit)
food.desc: Breadfruit buried and fermented in leaf-lined pits until sharp and tangy, then baked into dense cakes. A traditional way to store food on a coral atoll.

places.name: Babes Place
places.note: One of the few places serving fermented breadfruit to visitors rather than only within families.

places.name: Bairiki Market food stalls
places.note: Traditional preserved foods turn up at the market stalls; a good place to try small portions.

places.name: Bikenibeu Market
places.note: Eastern South Tarawa market with home-cooked island foods sold from mid-morning.

food.name: Te Babai (Giant Swamp Taro)
food.desc: Enormous corms grown for years in hand-dug pits, cooked and mashed with coconut cream. A prestige food reserved for feasts and important guests.

places.name: Babes Place
places.note: Traditional menu that includes the pit crops rarely served commercially.

places.name: Otintaai Hotel Restaurant
places.note: Serves te babai and other traditional dishes at cultural dinners and functions.

places.name: Bikenibeu Market
places.note: Taro and babai corms sold here, sometimes prepared as a coconut-cream mash.

food.name: Te Tuae (Dried Pandanus)
food.desc: Pandanus fruit pulp cooked down and sun-dried into sweet, leathery sheets that keep for years. Voyaging food, still eaten as a chewy snack.

places.name: Bairiki Market food stalls
places.note: Dried pandanus and pandanus flour sold in bundles at the main South Tarawa market.

places.name: Bikenibeu Market
places.note: Traditional preserved sweets from the outer islands often arrive here with inter-island boats.

places.name: Babes Place
places.note: Includes traditional sweets like te tuae alongside its main island dishes.

food.name: Te Karewe (Coconut Toddy)
food.desc: Sap tapped from the coconut spathe at dawn and dusk, drunk fresh and sweet. Toddy-cutting songs are part of daily life across the atoll.

places.name: Bairiki Market
places.note: Bottles of fresh toddy sold in the mornings; best drunk the same day before it ferments.

places.name: Babes Place
places.note: Serves fresh karewe and the boiled-down kamaimai syrup with traditional meals.

places.name: Bikenibeu Market
places.note: Toddy cutters sell along the road here at first light; ask for karewe rather than the fermented version.

food.name: Te Kabubu
food.desc: Roasted pandanus flour whisked into water or coconut milk into a nourishing, nutty drink. Traditional energy food for fishermen and nursing mothers.

places.name: Bairiki Market
places.note: Pandanus flour sold by the packet; stalls will mix it up fresh for you.

places.name: Babes Place
places.note: Traditional drinks served alongside island meals, kabubu among them.

places.name: Chatterbox Cafe
places.note: Cafe stop where local drinks appear beside coffee; convenient central meeting spot.

landmarks: Betio Island Battlefields

This small islet was the site of the brutal 1943 Battle of Tarawa, one of the Pacific War's bloodiest clashes, and remnants of that history are scattered across its shores. History buffs come to walk among rusting relics under the tropical sun.
Red Beach

The infamous WWII landing site where U.S. Marines stormed ashore in 1943 is now a quiet stretch of sand, its wartime past marked by memorials and the occasional relic still visible at low tide. It's a poignant, must-see spot for anyone interested in Pacific history.
Japanese Bunkers and Naval Guns, Betio

Massive rusted coastal defense guns and concrete bunkers still stand where Japanese forces made their last stand, hauntingly preserved by the salt air. These weathered relics offer a raw, tangible link to World War II in the Pacific.
Tarawa War Memorial
This memorial on Betio honors the thousands of American and Japanese soldiers who lost their lives in the 1943 battle. It's a solemn, reflective stop for visitors tracing the island's wartime legacy.
Tungaru National Museum and Cultural Centre

Kiribati's small but earnest national museum showcases traditional artifacts, canoes, and cultural displays that tell the story of the I-Kiribati people. It's the best introduction to local heritage beyond the war history.
Parliament House (Maneaba ni Maungatabu), Bairiki

Built in the style of a traditional maneaba meeting house, Kiribati's parliament building blends modern governance with local architectural tradition. Its distinctive thatched-style roofline stands out on the atoll.
Betio-Bairiki-Bonriki Causeway

This narrow ribbon of road strings together South Tarawa's islets across turquoise lagoon waters, offering some of the most scenic drives (or bike rides) in the country. Sunset views along the causeway are unforgettable.
South Tarawa Lagoon Beaches

Calm, shallow lagoon waters lined with swaying coconut palms make for idyllic swimming and photography, a striking contrast to the wilder ocean side of the atoll. Local outrigger canoes often dot the water at dawn.
London Village and Church, North Tarawa

A traditional Kiribati village accessible by boat or low-tide walk, where thatched-roof homes and a historic church reflect authentic island life away from the capital's bustle. It's a glimpse of untouched, old-style Kiribati.
Betio Sea Wall and Harbor
This bustling seawall and harbor area is the maritime heart of Kiribati, where inter-island boats, fishermen, and traders converge daily. It offers lively local color and sweeping ocean views.

train.note: There are no railways in Kiribati. South Tarawa is reached by air into Bonriki International Airport, with flights from Fiji, Nauru and Brisbane via Nauru Airlines and Fiji Airways. There is no rail anywhere in the country.

bus.note: No international coaches. Privately run minibuses shuttle constantly along the single causeway road that links the islets of South Tarawa from Betio to Bonriki - flag them down anywhere and pay a flat fare on board. This is the main form of transport and can be crowded and slow.

intl.to: Outer Gilbert Islands - Abaiang, Abemama & Butaritari (Kiribati) - irregular government and private vessels
intl.op: Kiribati Shipping Services — tickets at the Betio port

ferry.note: There is no scheduled international ferry. Small boats and government vessels connect Tarawa with the outer Gilbert Islands on irregular schedules announced locally, and the passenger boat between Betio and Bairiki saves the long causeway drive. Voyages to the Line Islands take days and run rarely.

half.name: Abaiang Atoll
half.blurb: Neighboring coral atoll reached by boat, with village life and a sheltered lagoon.

full.name: Maiana Atoll
full.blurb: Narrow coral atoll south of Tarawa reached by boat, with small villages along its lagoon shore.
